step_by_step_reasoning: 1) Nodes: all 11 World Model entities are kept. The user is kept as the system entry point. The two EC2 icons stay separate because they do different jobs (legacy application hosting vs. self-managed monitoring tools). 'Load Balancer' and 'Mongo DB' are mapped to ThirdParty as given in the World Model; Kafka, drawn on the same Mongo/Kafka box, is recorded in the Mongo node notes. 2) Ledger: visual_connections has 15 entries; each is emitted once with the same source and target, including all reverse directions (S3<->CloudFront, CloudFront<->Lambda, CloudFront<->Load Balancer, Load Balancer<->EKS, Load Balancer<->legacy EC2, EKS<->Mongo, EKS<->RDS). 3) Audio assigns flows: flow 0 = edge layer (user traffic, S3 static content, Lambda routing decision); flow 1 = load balancer routing to legacy EC2 or EKS microservices, data layer access and responses; flow 2 = monitoring. 4) Extra edges: the transcript says CloudWatch is used to check pod health and that self-managed tools (Prometheus, ELK) on EC2 give an internal look at every service, so 2 meta edges are added from EKS to CloudWatch and to the monitoring EC2 node; these are not in the ledger and are inferred from the monitoring description to avoid orphan nodes. 5) Self-check: visual_connections entries = 15; edges emitted = 17 (15 ledger + 2 audio-grounded monitoring edges).

graph.name: Seera Group: Scalable Microservices Travel Platform (Almosafer) on AWS
graph.categories: Microservices, Containers, Travel, Migration, Content Delivery
graph.notes: Seera Group's Almosafer travel platform receives about 300k requests per minute through CloudFront, with S3 for static content and Lambda for region/device routing decisions. Around 60 load balancers route traffic between frontend and backend and between legacy EC2 monoliths and EKS microservices (about 80% migrated; 250+ microservices on 1400+ pods). The data layer uses self-managed MongoDB on EC2, RDS for transactional SQL, and Kafka for event-driven services. Monitoring uses CloudWatch, Prometheus and ELK, with alerting through Slack and PagerDuty.

nodes.name: User
nodes.notes: Almosafer customers; about 300k requests per minute on average.

nodes.name: CloudFront
nodes.notes: CDN that receives all user traffic; first layer of scaling and resiliency.

nodes.name: S3
nodes.notes: Cost-efficient storage serving static content and images for a content-heavy platform.

nodes.name: Lambda
nodes.notes: Edge logic that determines which region and device the traffic comes from, to decide request routing.

nodes.name: Load Balancer
nodes.notes: About 60 load balancers; decide between backend service traffic and web (frontend) traffic, and route between legacy systems and new microservices.

nodes.name: EC2 Legacy Application
nodes.notes: Hosts the remaining legacy monolithic systems that are being gradually migrated to microservices.

nodes.name: EKS
nodes.notes: Core for all backend and micro-frontend services; about 80% of services migrated; 250+ microservices on 1400+ pods in production.

nodes.name: Mongo DB
nodes.notes: Self-managed MongoDB instances on EC2 for services needing NoSQL; Kafka, drawn on the same box, supports the event-driven microservices.

nodes.name: RDS
nodes.notes: Managed SQL database for services that need proper transactions.

nodes.name: EC2 Monitoring Tools
nodes.notes: Hosts self-managed monitoring tools such as Prometheus and the ELK stack for log monitoring; tied to alerting through Slack and PagerDuty.

nodes.name: CloudWatch
nodes.notes: AWS-native monitoring used to check pod health; tied to alerting through Slack and PagerDuty.

edges.notes: User traffic (about 300k requests per minute) goes through CloudFront.
CloudFront requests static content and images from S3.
S3 returns static content and images to CloudFront.
CloudFront invokes Lambda to evaluate the request's region and device.
Lambda returns the routing decision to CloudFront.
CloudFront forwards dynamic traffic to the load balancers.
Load balancer routes traffic to legacy systems on EC2.
Load balancer routes backend or frontend traffic to microservices on EKS.
Microservices read and write the self-managed MongoDB; event-driven services use Kafka.
MongoDB results (and Kafka events) return to the microservices.
Services that need transactions query RDS.
RDS returns query results to the microservices.
EKS services respond to the load balancer.
Legacy application responds to the load balancer.
Load balancer returns the response to CloudFront.
CloudWatch monitors pod health. Not a drawn arrow; inferred from the monitoring description.
Prometheus and ELK on EC2 monitor every service's metrics and logs. Not a drawn arrow; inferred from the monitoring description.
